definition: Indolent means habitually lazy; avoiding effort.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word indolent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know indolent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: By the second week of the heat wave the whole office had turned indolent, meetings drifting past their own agendas.
Unhurried is no vice at all — simply taking one's time — and it stops well short of indolent, which avoids the effort itself.
Slothful goes further than indolent, turning a lazy habit into something closer to a settled vice.

Idle describes a state, not a character: the machine, or the worker, is simply not working right now, for any reason at all. Indolent is a settled trait — effort avoided as a way of life. A diligent person can be idle on a Sunday; only a habit makes someone indolent.

Sluggish blames low energy: the body or system is moving slowly because there is little power behind it. The indolent have energy to spare and simply decline to spend it on work. A sluggish river cannot hurry; an indolent roommate could wash the dish and won't.
steadily hardworking by habit
full of vigor and eager to spend it
The basset hound kept up its doleful stare until the biscuit tin finally opened.
Indolent means habitually lazy; avoiding effort.
My roommate Dev is brilliant and indolent in equal measure: he microwaves dinner in the same bowl he'll eat from, purely to spare himself the washing of one dish.
Indolent is a settled disposition — effort avoided on principle — not a mood.
Listless people lack energy from illness or gloom; weary people have spent theirs.
The indolent are fine; they simply decline the work.
Latin in- ('not') + dolere ('to feel pain'): the word slid from painless to comfortable to work-shy.
Indolent paints laziness as a settled trait, with a faintly amused, literary tone — an indolent cat, an indolent August.
Lazy is blunter; listless and sluggish blame energy, not character.
Doctors keep the old painless sense: an indolent condition advances slowly and quietly.

Every allotment garden has its legend, and on the Marsh Lane plots the legend was Desmond.
Desmond was not weak and not tired.
He biked eleven miles to the plots each Saturday, played two hard sets of badminton by the gate, and then settled into a folding chair beside a bed of weeds he had no intention of pulling.
The committee called him indolent, and the word was chosen with care: his neighbors worked; Desmond supervised his own comfort.
Offers of help embarrassed him into half an hour of hoeing, after which the chair reclaimed him.
When the plot inspection came, Desmond charmed the inspectors so thoroughly that they left believing the thistles were a pollinator project.
